sn19.14:1.1: _Maṅguli_ is unclear. It is perhaps related to _maṅgura_ as a skin color, neither black nor brown, where the corresponding Sanskrit term is _madgura_, also spelled _maṅgura_. This is a species of fish, probably the common catfish *clarias magur*, which has a dingy greenish or muddy color.
sn19.14:1.4: _Ikkhaṇikā_ (Sanskrit _īkṣaṇikā_) is literally a “seeress”, but her putative powers extend beyond mere visions of the future. What she sees are _maṅgala_ (“auspicies”), hence she is reborn like a _maṅguli_ (“catfish”). Such fortune-tellers were considered a “thorn” to society alongside dissemblers, cheats, gamblers, and palmists (Manu 9.258). Medhātithi comments that they would con wealthy men out of money by promising them the favors of the gods, or casting spells. Thus the word comes full circle to approximate the modern sense of “catfishing”. Nonetheless, Kautilya, ever the pragmatist, is not above enlisting them in the services of the state for the dissemination of fake news (Arthaśāstra 13.1.7). Jain texts say she worked by jingling a small bell under her ear, at the sound of which her tutelary spirit would approach and whisper secrets. The background story to [ja126]() tells how such a fortune-teller was enlisted by a princess to deploy faked magical powers to ensure she would end up with her lover. Her claimed powers in this story include divination of possession, exorcism, and revivifying a corpse with a malevolent spirit.
